The name “Lassen” appears in the Encyclopaedia Britannica, in the entry “Arab,” alongside Renan. Both are described as having attributed special characteristics to the “Semitic race.” The article answers them by arguing that these traits did not arise from the nature of Semites “as a race,” but from particular features of the environment in which they lived. Had they lived in a different environment and under different conditions, they would have developed different characteristics from those attributed to them.↩︎

Hegel believes that religion uses art as a form of “absolute spirit,” and that both religion and art operate through sensory representations. Here we should recall the familiar distinction between two stages of knowledge: sensory and rational. The first develops through sensations, perceptions, and representations. The second develops through concepts, judgments, and conclusions.↩︎

We do not deny that Arab-Islamic philosophy took religious forms. Like other medieval philosophies, it was tied to religious history. But this real feature does not conceal its materialist tendencies. Medieval philosophers were able to express their materialist philosophical inclinations through religious forms—sometimes openly, as with Ibn Sina, and sometimes through symbolism or strategic maneuvering.↩︎
